title: Water goes up
summary: Before rain can fall, water has to reach the sky. It travels there as a gas you cannot see.

blocks.text: Every raindrop starts as water on the ground. To fall from the sky, it first has to get up there, and it makes the trip as a gas.
[[Evaporation]] is the change from liquid water into water vapour, a gas. It happens when heat breaks the bonds that hold water molecules together.
The vapour mixes into the air and cannot be seen. The water has not gone anywhere: it is now part of the air around us.
About 90 percent of the moisture in the air came from water evaporating from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers.
Oceans cover more than 70 percent of Earth's surface, which is why so much of that moisture comes from them.

blocks.alt: Sun shines on the sea; dotted wavy lines show water vapour rising, an arrow carries it to a cloud over the land, and rain falls from the cloud.
blocks.caption: Heat turns water into vapour, the vapour is carried up into a cloud, and the cloud can rain on the land.

blocks.text: The next lesson follows this vapour as it rises, cools and turns back into liquid by [[condensation]]. That is how a cloud is made. You can read ahead in the [glossary](glossary:condensation) or go to [lesson 2](lesson:clouds#rising-air-cools).

takeaways: Evaporation turns liquid water into water vapour, an invisible gas.
It needs heat to break the bonds between water molecules.
Oceans, seas, lakes and rivers supply about 90 percent of the moisture in the air.
recap: Rain starts as water on the ground.
Heat turns it into water vapour, a gas you cannot see.
Most of that vapour comes from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers.

quiz.question: What is evaporation?
options: Water vapour turning into liquid water
Liquid water turning into water vapour
quiz.proof: Evaporation is the change from liquid water into water vapour, a gas.

quiz.question: Where did about 90 percent of the moisture in the air come from?
quiz.proof: About 90 percent of the moisture in the air came from water evaporating from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers.
